meta.titre: Motion: velocity, acceleration and the equations of motion

sections.contenu_markdown: A minibus leaves the motor park in Douala, speeds up along the road to Edea, then brakes hard at a police checkpoint. Every part of that journey can be described by a few quantities: distance, speed, velocity and acceleration. At the GCE O/L, motion questions ask you to read graphs and ticker tapes, and to use the equations of uniformly accelerated motion for vehicles, runners and falling stones. They are marks you can win with a clear method.

items: Distance is measured in metres (m) and time in seconds (s).
Speed is distance divided by time, and $1\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}} = \dfrac{1}{3.6}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.
The acceleration due to gravity near the Earth's surface is taken as $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

sections.titre: Describing motion: speed, acceleration, graphs and equations
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Speed** is the distance travelled per unit time. **Velocity** is speed in a stated direction. **Acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity:

$$a = \frac{v - u}{t}$$

where $u$ is the initial velocity, $v$ the final velocity and $t$ the time taken. Its unit is $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. A negative acceleration is called a deceleration (retardation).

For **uniform acceleration** in a straight line:

$$v = u + at \qquad s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2 \qquad v^2 = u^2 + 2as \qquad s = \frac{(u + v)}{2}\,t$$

**Reading graphs**

| Graph | Gradient | Area under the graph |
|---|---|---|
| Distance-time | speed | none used |
| Velocity-time | acceleration | distance travelled |

A horizontal line on a velocity-time graph means constant velocity (zero acceleration). A straight sloping line means constant acceleration. A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means the body is at rest.

**Free fall.** When air resistance is ignored, every falling body has the same constant acceleration $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. The velocity increases by $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ every second, but the acceleration does not change.

variantes.nom: Free fall and objects thrown upward
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a body is dropped or thrown vertically and air resistance is ignored.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use the same equations with $a = g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for a body falling downward. A body dropped from rest has $u = 0$, so $v = gt$ and $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$. For a body thrown upward, it decelerates at $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ until it stops at the top ($v = 0$), then falls back.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the motion of a trolley is recorded as dots on a tape by a ticker timer.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A timer of frequency $50\ \mathrm{Hz}$ prints a dot every $0.02\ \mathrm{s}$. Equally spaced dots mean constant velocity. Dots whose spacing grows steadily mean uniform acceleration. For any section, speed $=$ length of the section $\div$ time, where time $=$ number of dot-spaces $\times\ 0.02\ \mathrm{s}$.

sections.enonce_markdown: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at $2.5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ for $8\ \mathrm{s}$. It then travels at constant velocity for $10\ \mathrm{s}$ and finally brakes uniformly to rest in $5\ \mathrm{s}$. Find (a) the maximum speed, (b) the total distance travelled, (c) the deceleration and (d) the average speed for the whole journey.

etapes.action: Find the maximum speed at the end of the acceleration.
Find the distance in each of the three stages.
etapes.justification: Use $s = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$ for the first stage, speed $\times$ time for the constant stage and the average speed $\times$ time for the braking stage.
Total distance is the sum of the distances of the stages.
The velocity falls from $20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to $0$ in $5\ \mathrm{s}$.
Average speed is total distance divided by total time ($8 + 10 + 5 = 23\ \mathrm{s}$).

sections.conclusion_markdown: The maximum speed is **20 m/s**, the total distance is **330 m**, the deceleration is **4 m/s squared** and the average speed is about **14.3 m/s**.

items.erreur_markdown: A student finds the acceleration of a body by reading the gradient of its distance-time graph.
items.pourquoi_faux: The gradient of a distance-time graph is the speed. Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph.
items.correction_markdown: Use distance-time gradient for speed; use velocity-time gradient for acceleration, and area under it for distance.

items.erreur_markdown: A student states: "The longer a stone falls, the larger its $g$ becomes."
items.pourquoi_faux: The velocity of the stone increases, but $g$ is a constant. A graph of $g$ against time is a horizontal line.
items.correction_markdown: Say that the stone's velocity grows by $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ each second while its acceleration stays at $10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.

items.erreur_markdown: A student puts $u = 54$ into $v = u + at$ for a car travelling at $54\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}$ with $t$ in seconds.
items.pourquoi_faux: The units are mixed: km/h and seconds cannot be combined in the equations of motion.

items.erreur_markdown: A braking car is described by $0 = 25 + 5t$ and the student gets $t = -5\ \mathrm{s}$.
items.pourquoi_faux: A deceleration must be entered as a negative acceleration. Using $+5$ for braking gives a negative, meaningless time.

items.enonce_markdown: A cyclist increases her speed uniformly from $2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ to $8\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in $3\ \mathrm{s}$ along a straight road. Calculate (a) her acceleration and (b) the distance she covers in these $3\ \mathrm{s}$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $a = \dfrac{v - u}{t} = \dfrac{8 - 2}{3} = 2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. **Acceleration = 2 m/s squared.**

(b) With uniform acceleration the average velocity is $\dfrac{2 + 8}{2} = 5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, so $s = 5 \times 3 = 15\ \mathrm{m}$. **Distance = 15 m.**

items.enonce_markdown: A stone is dropped from rest from the top of a cliff and reaches the sea after $3\ \mathrm{s}$. Ignoring air resistance and taking $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, find (a) the speed with which it hits the sea and (b) the height of the cliff.

A bus travelling at $25\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ is brought to rest by brakes giving a constant deceleration of $5\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$. (a) How long does it take to stop, and how far does it travel while braking? (b) The driver needs $0.8\ \mathrm{s}$ to react before pressing the brake pedal and the bus keeps its speed during that time. Find the total stopping distance.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $v = u + at$ with $v = 0$ and $a = -5$: $0 = 25 - 5t$, so $t = 5\ \mathrm{s}$.

$v^2 = u^2 + 2as$: $0 = 25^2 + 2(-5)s$, so $s = \dfrac{625}{10} = 62.5\ \mathrm{m}$. **Braking: 5 s and 62.5 m.**

(b) During the reaction time the bus moves at constant speed: $25 \times 0.8 = 20\ \mathrm{m}$.

Total stopping distance $= 20 + 62.5 = 82.5\ \mathrm{m}$. **Total stopping distance = 82.5 m.**

items_markdown: Speed is distance per unit time; velocity includes direction; acceleration is $a = (v - u)/t$ in $\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$.
Learn the four equations: $v = u + at$, $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^2$, $v^2 = u^2 + 2as$ and $s = \tfrac{(u+v)}{2}t$.
On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed; on a velocity-time graph the gradient is the acceleration and the area is the distance.
In free fall without air resistance, $g = 10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$ is constant: the velocity changes, the acceleration does not.
Convert units (km/h to m/s, minutes to seconds) before substituting, and enter a deceleration as a negative acceleration.
